old: I am who I am—after long wandering and great hardship, I’ve come home in the twentieth year to my own country.
new: Such as I am, it is I who, after long wandering and great hardship, have come home in the twentieth year to my own country.
reason: Butler: "Such as I am, it is I, who after long wandering and much hardship have got home in the twentieth year". This is Odysseus's claim of identity (it is I, changed as I am), and the draft turns it into a tautology that echoes the divine self-naming of Exodus 3:14, straight after he has told Telemachus "I am no god".

old: “What ship brought you here to Ithaca, dear father? What crew did they claim to be? You certainly couldn’t have come on foot.”
new: “In what ship, my dear father, did your crew bring you to Ithaca, and what people did they say they were?—for you can’t have come here by land.”
reason: Butler: "In what ship, my dear father, did your crew bring you to Ithaca? Of what nation did they declare themselves to be—for you cannot have come by land?" The draft replaces the question about nationality with "What crew did they claim to be?", which makes no sense, and adds "certainly". Accepted B01-P012 ("what people they said they were—for you cannot have come by land") and B14-P009 ("for you can’t have come here by land") fix this formula.

old: Now you’re consuming his property without payment, courting his wife, and trying to kill his son.
new: Now you’re consuming his property without paying for it, and you break my heart by courting his wife and trying to kill his son.
reason: Butler: "now you devour his property without paying for it, and break my heart by wooing his wife and trying to kill his son". The draft drops "break my heart", Penelope's own grief at the centre of her rebuke, The drafter repaired this paragraph and did not catch the omission.

old: because the dogs are being friendly and not barking
new: because the dogs are wagging their tails at him and not barking
reason: Butler repeats "fawned upon him" (P0) and "fawning upon him" (P1) on purpose: Odysseus is reading the dogs. P0 renders it "wagged their tails at him", and P1's "being friendly" breaks the repetition.

old: He certainly didn’t come here on foot.
new: He certainly didn’t come here by land.
reason: Butler: "for assuredly he did not come here by land". Accepted B01-P012 and B14-P009 keep "by land" in this recurring formula, and P22 repeats it.

old: “My boy, I’ll tell you the real truth.
new: “My son, I’ll tell you the real truth.
reason: Butler: "My son, I will tell you the real truth". This is Butler's own word (D29), and it is the swineherd's fatherly address, which the scene has just set up in P2's simile of a father welcoming his son.

old: a good cloak and tunic
new: a good cloak and shirt
reason: Butler: "a cloak and shirt of good wear". "shirt" is the edition's steady word (B14-P008, P020, P032 and more than twenty others), and this Book keeps "shirt" at P16.

old: serving women dragged around the house improperly, wine wasted recklessly
new: men dragging the serving women around the house in an unseemly way, wine drawn recklessly
reason: Butler: "men dragging the women servants about the house in an unseemly way, wine drawn recklessly, and bread wasted". The passive drops the agents and softens the sexual charge. It also merges Butler's "drawn" with the "wasted" of the next clause.

old: overrun with countless enemies
new: overrun with countless marauders
reason: Butler: "in the hands of numberless marauders". "enemies" loses the concrete sense of plundering (Voice and form: concrete nouns are not generalized).

old: All the nobles from the neighboring islands
new: All the chiefs from the neighboring islands
reason: Butler: "the chiefs from all the neighbouring islands". This is the same list as B01-P016, which accepted Book 1 renders "The chiefs from all our islands", and GLOSSARY holds "chief" (rank) steady.

old: your appearance has completely altered
new: your color is not the same
reason: Butler: "your colour is not the same". The draft intensifies ("completely") and loses the echo of P16's "She restored his color".

old: offerings of fine gold
new: offerings of worked gold
reason: Butler: "offerings of wrought gold". Accepted B13-P001 renders Butler's "wrought gold" as "worked gold", while "fine gold" is the edition's rendering of a different phrase (B08-P033).

old: the work of the great goddess Athena
new: the work of the formidable goddess Athena
reason: Butler: "the redoubtable goddess Minerva". Accepted B03-P029 and B13-P028 render redoubtable as "formidable", and "great" flattens it.

old: so we can plan the destruction of our enemies
new: so we can plan how to kill our enemies
reason: Butler: "that we may consult about killing our enemies". The rules forbid softening violence.

old: First, give me a count of the suitors and their numbers, so I can consider whether
new: First, give me a list of the suitors and their number, so I may learn who they are and how many. Then I can turn the matter over in my mind and see whether
reason: Butler: "give me a list of the suitors, with their number, that I may learn who, and how many, they are. I can then turn the matter over in my mind". The draft drops "who" (a list of names) and says the count twice.

old: you may bitterly regret coming here for revenge
new: you may bitterly regret your coming and your revenge
reason: Butler: "you may have bitter cause to rue your coming, and your revenge". The revenge is itself something to rue; the draft turns it into a purpose clause.

old: are certainly good allies
new: are a good pair of allies
reason: Butler: "are a couple of good allies". The draft adds an intensifier and drops the understatement.

old: Furthermore, remember this carefully: when
new: Furthermore I say—and take my words to heart—when
reason: Butler: "Furthermore I say, and lay my saying to your heart". Accepted B11-P037 fixes this recurring formula as "Furthermore I say—and take my words to heart—", and it recurs in Books 17 and 19.

old: for their day of reckoning has come
new: for their day of reckoning is at hand
reason: Butler: "the day of their reckoning is at hand". It is near, not arrived; the fight is still days off.

old: you’ll come to know my character in time
new: you’ll come to know me in time
reason: Butler: "you will come to know me by and by". "my character" is added, and it weakens the line in a recognition scene.

old: wasting your estate freely and without remorse
new: wasting your estate with impunity and without remorse
reason: Butler: "with impunity and without compunction". "freely" drops the idea of going unpunished, which is the point the suitors will pay for.

old: Their servants took their weapons
new: Their servants took their armor
reason: Butler: "their servants came and took their armour from them". Accepted B04-P071 keeps "armor" in the same ship scene (D29: Butler's word).

old: surrounding the outer courtyard and held a meeting near the main gate
new: surrounding the outer court and held a council near the main gate
reason: Butler: "the outer court, and held a council". Accepted Books keep "outer court" (B01-P031, B02-P019, B04-P059, B07-P010) and "council" (B09-P008, B10-P013, B12-P024), and this draft restored "council" at P24.

old: “Friends,” he said, “this voyage of Telemachus’s is a serious matter.
new: “My friends,” he said, “this voyage of Telemachus’s is a very serious matter.
reason: Butler: "My friends ... this voyage of Telemachus's is a very serious matter". The accepted Books keep "My friends" (B10-P013, B11-P029, B12-P012), and the draft drops "very".

old: their servants took their weapons
new: their servants took their armor
reason: Butler: "their servants took their armour from them". This is the same line as P29 and B04-P071.

old: our plan will never succeed while he’s alive
new: our plan is never likely to succeed while he’s alive
reason: Butler: "our affair is never likely to come off while he is alive". The draft drops the hedge.

old: She can marry whoever offers the most and has the best luck.
new: She can marry whoever offers the most for her and whose lot it is to win her.
reason: Butler: "the man who will give the most for her, and whose lot it is to win her". "lot" is what is allotted or fated, and "the best luck" reduces it to chance.

old: “Friends,” he said, speaking
new: “My friends,” he said, speaking
reason: Butler: "My friends," said he. This matches P31 and the accepted Books.

old: It’s a terrible thing to kill someone of noble blood.
new: It’s a heinous thing to kill someone of noble blood.
reason: Butler: "It is a heinous thing". The word is current English, and "terrible" softens the moral charge (D29).

old: and scolded Antinous:
new: and rebuked Antinous:
reason: Butler: "rebuked Antinous". "scolded" diminishes a queen's public rebuke to domestic nagging.

old: though Eumaeus couldn’t see him
new: taking care that Eumaeus couldn’t see him
reason: Butler: "but so that Eumaeus could not see him". The concealment is deliberate, and "though" reports it as chance.

old: enjoyed the gift of sleep
new: enjoyed the boon of sleep
reason: Butler: "enjoyed the boon of sleep". Accepted B04-P022 keeps "boon of sleep", and the formula recurs at B19 and B23.

old: despite a man like you being here
new: even with a man like you present
reason: "despite ... being here" is a legal but slightly clotted gerund construction; a listener has to work a beat to parse who is 'here' and why it's a 'despite.' Not blocking, just a small stumble.

old: If they outnumbered me—being alone—I’d rather die fighting
new: If I stood alone against so many, I’d rather die fighting
reason: The parenthetical '—being alone—' sits right after 'they outnumbered me,' so on a first hearing it can briefly seem to describe 'they' rather than 'me.' A listener has to backtrack to attach it correctly.

old: No other Odysseus will come after this.
new: There is no other Odysseus to come after this one.
reason: Standing alone, this reads as a claim about the future (implying some other man named Odysseus might otherwise show up), when the intended sense is 'this is truly me, not a substitute.' A first-time listener is likely to momentarily misread the point of the sentence.

old: my spear will be red with his blood, for many times Odysseus took me on his knees
new: my spear will be red with that man’s blood, for many times Odysseus took me on his knees
reason: 'his blood' most immediately points back to 'your son Telemachus,' the closest preceding referent, so on first hearing this sounds like Eurymachus threatening to kill Telemachus — the opposite of what he means (that he'll kill anyone who threatens Telemachus). The very next sentence ('Telemachus is my dearest friend') clarifies, but only after the misreading has already happened. [lead: “that man” = the one who would lay hands on Telemachus, as in Butler; nothing added]
